limitations_and_boundaries: The study focuses on Hydra regeneration from excised tissue fragments; applicability to other organisms or developmental contexts is not established.
The causal relationship between topological defects and morphogenesis is correlative; direct manipulation of defects was not performed.
The analysis primarily considers the ectodermal actin fibers; endodermal fibers are noted but not extensively characterized.
The role of biochemical signaling pathways in conjunction with mechanical cues is hypothesized but not experimentally dissected.

research_questions.statement: How does the nematic organization of supracellular actin fibers relate to morphogenesis during Hydra regeneration?

provenance.text_excerpt: Importantly, the topological defects in mature Hydra coincide with the morphological features of the animal. Specifically, two +1 point defects are found at the apex of the head and foot regions: a +1 defect at the tip of the mouth (hypostome; Fig. 1c), and a +1 defect at the base of the foot, surrounding the basal disc (Fig. 1d). ... each tentacle has a +1 defect at its tip (Fig. 1e) that is accompanied by two −1/2 defects at opposite sides of its base (Fig. 1f).

claims.statement: In mature Hydra, topological defects in the nematic actin fiber field coincide with morphological features: +1 defects at head and foot apices, and tentacles contain +1 and -1/2 defects.

experiments_or_tasks: Imaging of actin fibers in mature Hydra using lifeact-GFP transgenic animals to characterize nematic order and topological defects.

methods.name: Live fluorescence microscopy
methods.protocol_description: Transgenic Hydra expressing lifeact-GFP in the ectoderm were imaged to visualize supracellular actin fibers. Nematic director field and topological defects were identified from fiber orientation.

study_units.name: Nematic organization in mature Hydra

provenance.text_excerpt: Specifically, two +1 point defects are found at the apex of the head and foot regions: a +1 defect at the tip of the mouth (hypostome; Fig. 1c), and a +1 defect at the base of the foot, surrounding the basal disc (Fig. 1d). ... each tentacle has a +1 defect at its tip (Fig. 1e) that is accompanied by two −1/2 defects at opposite sides of its base (Fig. 1f).

results.value_raw_text: Mature Hydra have two +1 point defects at the head and foot apices, and a variable number of tentacles each with a +1 defect at the tip and two -1/2 defects at the base.

provenance.text_excerpt: The total defect charge of a tentacle is thus equal to 0, and hence does not contribute to the net defect charge in the animal.

results.value_raw_text: Total defect charge in mature Hydra equals +2, with tentacles contributing net zero charge.

provenance.text_excerpt: Together, these findings indicate that it is possible to discern the sites where +1 defects will emerge at very early stages of the regeneration process. These sites remain stationary with respect to the tissue and hence identify the region of cells that will eventually form the functional morphological features of the regenerated animal ... Importantly, there is a clear asymmetry between the head- and foot-forming processes: early +1 defects become the site of head formation, whereas two +1/2 defects merge at the site that becomes the foot of the regenerated animal (Fig. 4).

claims.statement: During Hydra regeneration, topological defects in the nematic actin fiber field act as organization centers for morphogenesis, with early +1 defects marking head formation and merging +1/2 defects marking foot formation.

provenance.text_excerpt: On the basis of our results, we suggest a complementary view of morphogenesis in which a physical field (here, the nematic actin fibre orientation) can be considered as a mechanical morphogen field that provides relevant cues for directing the morphogenesis process.

claims.statement: The nematic orientation field can be considered a 'mechanical morphogen' whose dynamics, in conjunction with biochemical signaling, lead to robust functional patterning during morphogenesis.

experiments_or_tasks: Excision of tissue fragments from transgenic Hydra expressing lifeact-GFP, followed by live imaging of actin dynamics during regeneration into spheroids and subsequent morphogenesis.

methods.name: Live time-lapse microscopy of regenerating tissue spheroids
methods.protocol_description: Tissue fragments were excised from the gastric region of transgenic Hydra expressing lifeact-GFP in the ectoderm. Folding into spheroids occurred within hours. Actin fiber organization and topological defects were tracked over 2-3 days of regeneration.

study_units.name: Nematic organization during regeneration from excised tissue fragments

additional_provenance.text_excerpt: These +1 defects remain stationary relative to the underlying tissue and can be followed throughout the regeneration process, at the end of which they will predominantly be located at the mouth of the regenerated animal (Fig. 4a,d and Supplementary Video 4). Alternatively, +1 defects can arise through merging, when two +1/2 defects aligned with their curved ends facing each other move closer together as the tissue elongates, until they coalesce, most typically to form the foot (Fig. 4b,e and Supplementary Video 5).

provenance.text_excerpt: Owing to the topological constraint of the closed surface, fibre alignment cannot be continuous everywhere and topological defects in the nematic order must emerge (Fig. 2a). As the extended disordered regions progressively become ordered, the topological defects appear.

results.value_raw_text: Topological defects emerge from disordered regions as order expands; +1/2 and -1/2 defects appear, with +1/2 defects being motile and eventually merging or forming +1 defects.

provenance.text_excerpt: The formation of holes in regenerating spheroids is never observed within regions containing ordered nematic fibre alignment (Fig. 4f). Instead, the ruptures occur in disordered regions (Fig. 4f) during the earlier stages of regeneration before localized point defects develop. ... At later times, after localized defects appear, hole formation occurs almost exclusively at +1 defect sites (Fig. 4c,f).

results.value_raw_text: Rupture holes occur in disordered regions early, and later almost exclusively at +1 defect sites.

provenance.text_excerpt: Importantly, there is a clear asymmetry between the head- and foot-forming processes: early +1 defects become the site of head formation, whereas two +1/2 defects merge at the site that becomes the foot of the regenerated animal (Fig. 4).

results.value_raw_text: Early +1 defects become sites of head formation; two +1/2 defects merge to form the foot.

results.metric_name: Fraction of spheroid surface with ordered nematic fibers

provenance.text_excerpt: We find that the ordered nematic fibre array occupies roughly half of the spheroid’s surface area, whereas the remaining surface is essentially devoid of aligned fibres (Fig. 2b, left). ... During approximately the first 24 h after excision, nematic arrays of actin fibres gradually form in the previously disordered regions ... and the fraction of the spheroids’ surface area that contains ordered fibre arrays increases to span nearly the entire surface (Fig. 2b,c).

results.value_raw_text: Initially, ordered nematic fiber array occupies roughly half of the spheroid's surface area; within ~24 h, ordered regions expand to span nearly the entire surface.
